props.title: Dragnet

sections.content: **Dragnet** (1954) marks a pivotal transition from radio and television to the big screen, with Jack Webb's iconic Joe Friday delivering his "just the facts" approach to police procedurals. The film builds on the massive success of the TV series (1951-1959) while amplifying its signature documentary-style realism. Webb's directing and starring role established a template for police procedurals that influenced everything from **The French Connection** (1971) to **Law & Order** (1990-present). The film's methodical pacing, authentic LAPD locations, and focus on the mundane details of police work created a stark contrast to the more sensationalized crime films of the era like **White Heat** (1949).

sections.content: The film's influence extends far beyond its immediate era. Its documentary approach and partnership dynamics echo through films like **Training Day** (2001) and **End of Watch** (2012). Webb's deadpan delivery and commitment to procedural accuracy created a new standard for police films, moving away from the noir stylization of the 1940s toward a grittier realism that would later influence directors like Sidney Lumet with **Serpico** (1973) and William Friedkin with **The French Connection** (1971). SUBHEAD: The Documentary-Style Crime Film Legacy

Dragnet's revolutionary blend of entertainment and education spawned numerous imitators and evolved the police procedural genre. Its DNA can be found in films like **The New Centurions** (1972), **Prince of the City** (1981), and even modern procedurals like **Zodiac** (2007). The film's commitment to showing the day-to-day reality of police work, including mundane details and bureaucratic procedures, created a new paradigm for crime storytelling that continues to influence filmmakers today.
